topical-and-factor-hemostasis.title: Match Hemostatic Therapy to the Bleeding Site and Defect
topical-and-factor-hemostasis.summary: Topical thrombin and fibrin sealants act at a bleeding surface. Systemic factor replacement and inhibitor-bypassing therapies address specific coagulation defects. Match the product and route to the mechanism, then assess both clinical bleeding and the relevant monitoring results.
topical-and-factor-hemostasis.application: Confirm the bleeding source, exact product, route, allergy and antibody history, indication and clinical response plan with the procedural or hematology team.

lesson.heading: Use topical thrombin for accessible oozing
lesson.body: RECOTHROM is recombinant thrombin for surface hemostasis when conventional techniques are ineffective or impractical for minor capillary or small-venule bleeding. It is not for massive or brisk arterial bleeding. Keep its transfer syringe and receptacle labeled for topical use; never inject it. The label covers adults and children at least one month old; safety and efficacy are not established in neonates.

lesson.heading: Screen recombinant thrombin before use
lesson.body: RECOTHROM is contraindicated with hypersensitivity to the product, its components or hamster proteins. Entry into the circulation can cause thrombosis. Apply the exact product with its approved delivery system and follow the preparation instructions; a transfer syringe does not establish an injectable route.

lesson.heading: Recognize bovine thrombin's antibody risk
lesson.body: THROMBIN-JMI is bovine topical thrombin. Do not re-expose someone with known or suspected antibodies to bovine thrombin or factor V, and screen for bovine-product hypersensitivity. Antibodies can interfere with hemostasis: factor V antibodies may cross-react with human factor V and cause bleeding. Monitor for abnormal coagulation, bleeding or thrombosis.

lesson.heading: Treat a fibrin sealant as its own product
lesson.body: TISSEEL combines human fibrinogen and thrombin for topical surgical use. Spray delivery can cause fatal gas embolism if pressure or distance is inappropriate. Use the compatible device, gas, pressure and distance specified for that procedure; minimally invasive delivery uses CO2 only. Do not spray if the minimum distance cannot be assured, and never inject intravascularly. Screen for aprotinin-related hypersensitivity. It is not for severe or brisk arterial or venous bleeding or injection into highly vascular tissue such as nasal mucosa. Neurosurgical or other confined-space use is not FDA-approved.

lesson.heading: Distinguish skin closure from hemostatic delivery
lesson.body: An acrylate or adhesive name does not define a safe route or indication. Topical skin adhesives hold suitable wound edges together; FDA guidance advises against their use in ongoing bleeding, infection or incompletely debrided wounds. Internal tissue adhesives and vascular hemostatic devices have different intended uses. Select the exact device and follow its instructions rather than substituting a skin adhesive for a surgical hemostat.

lesson.heading: Match replacement to the missing factor
lesson.body: COAGADEX supplies human factor X for hereditary factor X deficiency, including prophylaxis, bleeding treatment and perioperative management across mild, moderate and severe disease. ADYNOVATE supplies PEGylated recombinant factor VIII for adult and pediatric hemophilia A, including bleeding treatment, perioperative management and prophylaxis; it is not indicated for von Willebrand disease. Their shared role in bleeding care does not make them interchangeable; identify the deficiency and use its specialist dosing and monitoring plan.

lesson.heading: Investigate an inadequate replacement response
lesson.body: For COAGADEX, monitor factor X activity; unexpectedly low activity or continued bleeding despite an appropriate dose warrants factor X inhibitor testing. ADYNOVATE similarly requires factor VIII activity monitoring and inhibitor evaluation when response is inadequate. Check preparation, administration and the bleeding source as well. These factor-specific assessments differ from interpreting INR after recombinant VIIa. Screen replacement-product hypersensitivity: prior life-threatening COAGADEX reactions are contraindications; ADYNOVATE also excludes prior anaphylaxis to the product, ADVATE, mouse or hamster proteins, or its excipients.

lesson.heading: Distinguish inhibitor bypass from replacement
lesson.body: FEIBA is an anti-inhibitor coagulant complex used in hemophilia A or B with inhibitors for bleeding control, perioperative care and prophylaxis. Its label does not indicate it for factor-deficiency bleeding without factor VIII or IX inhibitors. Confirm inhibitor status and the exact hematology plan before substituting a product.

lesson.heading: Screen FEIBA combinations before administration
lesson.body: FEIBA is contraindicated with DIC, acute thrombosis or embolism, or prior severe product hypersensitivity. Its label limits a single dose to 100 units/kg and total daily exposure to 200 units/kg; these ceilings are not starting-dose recommendations. Systemic tranexamic acid or aminocaproic acid is not recommended within approximately 6 to 12 hours after FEIBA because of thrombotic risk. Concurrent emicizumab requires specialist assessment and close monitoring for thrombotic microangiopathy if FEIBA is necessary.

lesson.heading: Identify the factor VIIa indication
lesson.body: IV NOVOSEVEN RT is labeled for bleeding and perioperative care in adults and children with hemophilia A or B with inhibitors, congenital factor VII deficiency, or Glanzmann thrombasthenia refractory to platelet transfusion, with or without platelet antibodies. Acquired hemophilia is an adult indication. These defined populations do not establish routine use for every trauma or anticoagulant-associated bleed.

lesson.heading: Treat thrombosis risk as part of selection
lesson.body: NOVOSEVEN RT carries a boxed warning for serious arterial and venous thrombosis. Review other hemostatic agents and thrombotic risk with the specialist team. New thrombosis or laboratory evidence of intravascular coagulation calls for dose reduction or stopping treatment according to the clinical situation.

lesson.heading: Measure bleeding control directly
lesson.body: After NOVOSEVEN RT, PT/INR, aPTT and factor VII activity do not directly establish hemostatic success. Assess actual bleeding and the patient's response. In congenital factor VII deficiency, laboratory and antibody assessment still has a role when expected response is absent; do not replace clinical assessment with a normalized INR.

keyPoints: Topical thrombin must not be injected.
Factor replacement and inhibitor bypass are not interchangeable.
Antibody, allergy and thrombosis risks depend on the product.
Laboratory correction is not proof of bleeding control.

check.question: A prepared RECOTHROM transfer syringe is handed over for IV administration. What is the immediate correction?
choices: Stop: this product is for topical application only
Give it slowly through a central line
Dilute it to convert it into an IV product
Use the INR to select its IV dose
check.rationale: A syringe used for product transfer does not change the topical-only route; intravascular exposure can cause thrombosis. A slower rate or central line does not make injection safe. Dilution cannot change its topical-only route, and INR cannot supply a valid IV dose for this product.

antifibrinolytic-hemostasis.title: Use Antifibrinolytics With Route and Renal Discipline
antifibrinolytic-hemostasis.summary: Tranexamic acid and aminocaproic acid reduce fibrinolysis. Their value depends on a bleeding context in which fibrinolysis matters, while kidney clearance, thrombosis, seizure risk, and route errors define the safety boundary.
antifibrinolytic-hemostasis.application: For every antifibrinolytic, document the evidence-based indication, timing, dose, kidney adjustment, route, thrombotic context, neurologic monitoring, and stop rule.

lesson.heading: Block fibrinolysis deliberately
lesson.body: Both agents inhibit fibrinolysis and help preserve formed clot. Tranexamic acid occupies lysine-binding sites involved in plasminogen and plasmin interaction with fibrin; aminocaproic-acid labeling describes inhibition of plasminogen activators and, to a lesser degree, plasmin activity. Neither replaces source control, fibrinogen, platelets, coagulation factors, temperature correction, or treatment of the actual bleeding mechanism.

lesson.heading: Make tranexamic-acid route unmistakable
lesson.body: The FDA injection indication is short-term bleeding reduction in hemophilia during and after tooth extraction; trauma, other surgical, and obstetric regimens require their own evidence and protocols. Adjust for renal impairment. Clearly label the intravenous route and segregate from neuraxial medicines because accidental intrathecal or epidural administration has caused seizures, dysrhythmia, permanent injury, and death.

lesson.heading: Keep oral tranexamic acid distinct from injection
lesson.body: The oral tablet indication is cyclic heavy menstrual bleeding in females of reproductive potential, a different use from IV dental, trauma or postpartum treatment. The cited tablet label contraindicates combined hormonal contraception, active or previous thrombosis or thromboembolism, intrinsic thrombotic risk, and hypersensitivity. Retinal artery or vein occlusion has been reported; new visual or ocular symptoms require stopping treatment and prompt ophthalmic evaluation. Oral and IV dosing and renal tables must not be interchanged.

lesson.heading: Identify the labeled tranexamic-acid regimen
lesson.body: For hemophilia tooth extraction, the injection label uses 10 mg/kg actual body weight before extraction with replacement therapy, then 10 mg/kg three to four times daily for 2 to 8 days. Its dose-reduction instructions apply before and after extraction. For example, serum creatinine 3.5 mg/dL falls in the 2.83 to 5.66 mg/dL band: 10 mg/kg once daily. Do not transfer this dental regimen automatically to another bleeding indication.

lesson.heading: Match trauma treatment to the injury clock
lesson.body: For an adult bleeding or at risk of significant bleeding after trauma, the 2023 European guideline recommends TXA promptly and within 3 hours of injury: 1 g IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours. Do not delay eligible treatment for viscoelastic results. This is a guideline regimen outside the cited U.S. dental indication; continue definitive bleeding control and resuscitation.

lesson.heading: Recognize postpartum bleeding early
lesson.body: WHO 2025 links first-response treatment to objectively measured blood loss: at least 300 mL with an abnormal hemodynamic sign, or at least 500 mL, whichever occurs first within 24 hours of birth. Abnormal signs include pulse over 100/min, systolic pressure below 100 mmHg, diastolic pressure below 60 mmHg, or shock index over 1. Shock index is pulse divided by systolic pressure. Watch especially closely in the first 2 hours. These criteria support prompt treatment and referral; they do not automatically mandate surgery. Evidence is strongest for facility vaginal births, so interpret cesarean measurements and anesthesia-related vital-sign changes clinically.

lesson.heading: Separate postpartum treatment from routine prevention
lesson.body: WHO 2025 advises against routine TXA prophylaxis for all vaginal or cesarean births. It does not replace preventive uterotonics. This population-level recommendation preserves a role for clinical judgment when a high-risk patient is already bleeding before formal diagnostic thresholds are met. Treatment of established postpartum hemorrhage remains recommended. Store TXA separately from bupivacaine to reduce catastrophic neuraxial mix-ups.

lesson.heading: Use the postpartum treatment schedule
lesson.body: WHO recommends early IV TXA alongside standard care for postpartum hemorrhage after vaginal or cesarean birth. Start within 3 hours of birth: 1 g over 10 minutes; repeat 1 g if bleeding persists after 30 minutes or recurs within 24 hours of finishing the first dose. The clock starts at birth, not diagnosis; WHO does not support starting treatment beyond that window. Do not wait to confirm the bleeding source before eligible treatment. Continue uterotonics, resuscitation and source control, and screen for contraindications such as a thromboembolic event during pregnancy. This treatment schedule is not an instruction for routine prophylaxis or an 8-hour trauma infusion.

lesson.heading: Read concentration and infusion rate together
lesson.body: The current 100 mg/mL tranexamic-acid label lists 0.5 mL/min, never exceeding 1 mL/min, for undiluted administration. Its diluted rates are 5 mL/min at 10 mg/mL or 2.5 mL/min at 20 mg/mL. Each listed rate delivers 50 mg/min; the undiluted upper limit is 100 mg/min. Rapid administration can cause hypotension. Do not mix this product with blood or penicillin-containing solutions.

lesson.heading: Screen beyond the route
lesson.body: Tranexamic-acid injection is contraindicated with active intravascular clotting, subarachnoid hemorrhage or hypersensitivity. Avoid concomitant prothrombotic medicines, including factor IX complex and anti-inhibitor coagulant concentrates and hormonal contraception. Seizures can occur even with IV use, especially at high surgical doses or increased exposure; renal adjustment and neurologic monitoring remain necessary.

lesson.heading: Use aminocaproic acid only for fibrinolytic bleeding
lesson.body: Aminocaproic acid is primarily renally eliminated, and its renal clearance approximates endogenous creatinine clearance. Distinguish primary fibrinolysis from disseminated intravascular coagulation before treatment. The label prohibits use with active intravascular clotting and states it must not be used in DIC without concomitant heparin; this is not a routine instruction to treat all DIC with both medicines. Avoid upper-tract hematuria use unless the expected benefit outweighs the risk of obstructing renal or ureteric clots.

lesson.heading: Infuse aminocaproic acid deliberately
lesson.body: For acute bleeding from increased fibrinolysis, the label suggests 4 to 5 g in 250 mL diluent over the first hour, followed by 1 g/hour in 50 mL diluent, ordinarily for about 8 hours or until controlled. The 250 mg/mL stock requires dilution; do not give it as a rapid undiluted IV injection. Avoid concurrent factor IX complex or anti-inhibitor coagulant concentrates because thrombosis risk may increase. Reassess dosing in severe renal failure. With prolonged treatment, monitor CK and muscle symptoms; stop if CK rises.

keyPoints: Antifibrinolytics do not replace source control.
Tranexamic acid is intravenous only in the injection label.
Aminocaproic acid requires evidence of fibrinolytic bleeding.

check.question: A tranexamic-acid syringe is found unlabeled beside epidural medications. What is the correct response?
choices: Remove it and correct intravenous-route labeling and segregation before use
Leave it because the route is obvious
Administer it epidurally
Mix it with the local anesthetic
check.rationale: Current labeling requires clear intravenous-route labeling because neuraxial administration has caused fatal and serious events. An unlabeled syringe must be removed and identified before administration. A clear solution or familiar tray does not establish its contents or route. Epidural administration is contraindicated, and combining it with a local anesthetic creates a dangerous route error.

perioperative-stress-ulcer.title: Use Stress-Ulcer Prophylaxis Only While Risk Persists
perioperative-stress-ulcer.summary: Stress-related mucosal bleeding prevention is a temporary risk intervention. Coagulopathy, shock, and chronic liver disease are the clearest current risk factors, while enteral nutrition, ventilation, neurologic illness, and preexisting acid disease also inform the decision.
perioperative-stress-ulcer.application: Write the current risk factor, route, agent, reassessment date, stop rule, and any independent long-term acid indication.

lesson.heading: Separate ICU location from bleeding risk
lesson.body: The 2024 SCCM and ASHP guideline identifies coagulopathy, shock, and chronic liver disease as likely risk factors for clinically important stress-related upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Its evidence review did not establish ventilation alone as an independent risk factor. The 2026 contextualized guideline for adult ICUs in Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and the Nordic countries incorporates newer evidence. Its practical considerations say clinicians may consider mechanically ventilated patients potentially at risk and assess them individually. This is not a separate graded recommendation requiring prophylaxis for every ventilated patient. Earlier uncertainty does not prove that ventilated patients cannot benefit.

lesson.heading: Choose a low-dose preventive regimen
lesson.body: For critically ill adults with bleeding risk factors, the 2024 SCCM/ASHP guideline conditionally suggests either a proton pump inhibitor or a histamine-2 receptor antagonist as first-line prophylaxis, with moderate-certainty evidence. It also accepts enteral or intravenous delivery, with low-certainty evidence. Choose one appropriate low-dose agent and route after checking organ function, interactions, enteral access and the original indication; these recommendations do not call for routine combined PPI and H2RA therapy.

lesson.heading: Apply sepsis-specific guidance
lesson.body: For adults with sepsis or septic shock and gastrointestinal bleeding risk factors, the 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign conditionally suggests PPI prophylaxis rather than no prophylaxis, with moderate-certainty evidence. This recommendation compares PPI with no prophylaxis; it does not itself prove PPI superiority over H2 blockers or make prophylaxis automatic for every patient with sepsis. The rationale cites earlier comparative evidence favoring PPIs for bleeding prevention and identifies H2 blockers as a reasonable alternative when PPIs are unavailable. Keep risk assessment, dose selection and stopping rules explicit.

lesson.heading: Define low dose and distinguish active bleeding
lesson.body: SCCM/ASHP defines low-dose daily totals as at most 40 mg for pantoprazole, omeprazole or esomeprazole; 30 mg for lansoprazole; and 40 mg for famotidine. These are preventive dose categories, not a universal prescription: renal function and product-specific administration still matter. Active gastrointestinal bleeding requires its own evaluation and treatment pathway.

lesson.heading: Reassess famotidine when kidney function or cognition changes
lesson.body: Famotidine clearance falls with renal impairment. The cited tablet labeling recommends dose reduction below a creatinine clearance of 60 mL/min and warns about CNS reactions and QT prolongation in moderate or severe impairment. New delirium in an older patient warrants medication and renal-dose review alongside other causes. Thrombocytopenia was reported in fewer than 1% of trial patients; a falling platelet count requires evaluation rather than automatic attribution to the H2 blocker.

lesson.heading: Put PPI warnings in their exposure context
lesson.body: Pantoprazole labeling describes observational associations with C. difficile-associated diarrhea and osteoporosis-related fractures. The fracture signal is especially associated with multiple daily doses and treatment for a year or longer; it is not an estimate of fracture risk from a brief ICU course. Investigate persistent diarrhea and use the lowest appropriate dose for the required duration. These cautions reinforce reassessment without replacing the patient's bleeding-risk assessment.

lesson.heading: Account for feeding and neurologic illness
lesson.body: Enteral nutrition probably reduces clinically important stress-related upper gastrointestinal bleeding, but feeding does not remove persistent risk such as coagulopathy. SCCM/ASHP conditionally suggests prophylaxis for fed adults who remain at risk and separately for neurocritical-care adults; both recommendations have very low-certainty evidence. It suggests avoiding prophylaxis in low-risk, fed adults, also with very low certainty, and notes that concurrent prophylaxis and feeding may increase pneumonia risk. Keep population, bleeding risk and uncertainty explicit.

lesson.heading: Monitor the selected acid-suppressive treatment
lesson.body: The book describes thrombocytopenia and mental-status changes with H2 receptor antagonists, particularly in older patients or those with renal impairment, and notes that tolerance to their effect can occur. Its PPI tables list C. difficile-associated diarrhea and other adverse effects; fracture warnings concern high doses or prolonged exposure. Review new symptoms, renal function and the continuing indication. Reported associations with infection or pneumonia do not establish that acid suppression caused an individual patient's illness.

lesson.heading: Distinguish acid tolerance from a bleeding outcome
lesson.body: Repeated H2-blocker dosing can produce tolerance to acid suppression. Randomized volunteer studies documented diminished gastric-pH response over repeated famotidine or ranitidine exposure. That physiologic endpoint does not establish that an individual ICU patient's prophylaxis has failed. Reassess the indication and clinical course instead of automatically escalating beyond the preventive regimen.

lesson.heading: Interpret infection concerns alongside randomized evidence
lesson.body: In the 2024 REVISE trial of invasively ventilated adults, pantoprazole reduced clinically important upper gastrointestinal bleeding compared with placebo. Ventilator-associated pneumonia and C. difficile infection were similar between groups, and mortality was not significantly different. This does not prove zero infection risk, but it does not support presenting pneumonia as an inevitable consequence of a short preventive course. Match the evidence to the patient, indication and exposure duration.

lesson.heading: Preserve an independent treatment indication
lesson.body: A PPI used before ICU admission may be treating recent upper gastrointestinal bleeding, erosive esophagitis, a hypersecretory condition or H. pylori eradication. Reconcile that independent indication before stopping it, weighing benefit, adverse effects, interactions and the available route. If the history is unclear, clarify it instead of assuming the drug was started solely for ICU prophylaxis. Resolution of stress-ulcer risk alone does not establish that the other treatment should end.

lesson.heading: Stop when the reason ends
lesson.body: Assess the indication daily and discontinue stress-ulcer prophylaxis when its risk factors are no longer present. SCCM/ASHP specifically calls for review and discontinuation of unnecessary prophylaxis before transfer out of the ICU to prevent inappropriate continuation. Its suggestion against prophylaxis in low-risk, enterally fed adults has very low-certainty evidence. Reconcile any separate acid-treatment indication so that a prophylaxis stop rule does not remove justified treatment.

keyPoints: Assess ventilated patients individually; do not equate uncertain independent risk with no benefit.
Either low-dose PPI or H2RA can be used.
Daily discontinuation review is part of the prescription.

check.question: An extubated, stable, enterally fed ICU patient has no neurologic critical illness, coagulopathy, shock, chronic liver disease, or separate acid indication. What is the best action?
choices: Discontinue routine stress-ulcer prophylaxis
Continue lifelong prophylaxis because the patient was ventilated
Double the acid-suppressive dose
Combine a PPI and H2RA
check.rationale: This low-risk, enterally fed patient has no remaining stated bleeding risk or independent acid-treatment indication. SCCM/ASHP conditionally suggests avoiding prophylaxis in this population, with very low-certainty evidence, and calls for stopping it when risk factors resolve. Prior ventilation does not justify lifelong treatment, a higher dose or routine combined PPI and H2RA therapy. Reassess if the clinical risk changes.

supplementalStressUlcerHeadings: Reassess famotidine when kidney function or cognition changes
Put PPI warnings in their exposure context
Distinguish acid tolerance from a bleeding outcome
Interpret infection concerns alongside randomized evidence

periop-antifib-route.question: An unlabeled syringe believed to contain tranexamic acid is on an epidural tray. What action is appropriate?
choices: Administer it epidurally at a lower dose
Use it if the solution is clear
Remove it from use and correct identification, IV-route labeling and segregation
Assume the tray establishes the route
periop-antifib-route.rationale: Tranexamic-acid injection must not be administered neuraxially; route errors have caused fatal seizures and arrhythmias. Lowering the dose does not make epidural delivery permissible. Clarity does not identify a medicine, and its presence on a tray cannot establish the safe route.

periop-antifib-renal.question: For the labeled hemophilia tooth-extraction indication, which tranexamic-acid schedule corresponds to serum creatinine 3.5 mg/dL?
choices: 10 mg/kg IV once daily
10 mg/kg IV four times daily without adjustment
10 mg/kg IV every hour
Use the dental regimen for every trauma patient
periop-antifib-renal.rationale: The 2.83 to 5.66 mg/dL label band uses 10 mg/kg daily. This is an indication-specific label table, not a universal trauma regimen. Four daily doses without adjustment ignore this renal band. An hourly schedule is not the label regimen. The dental table cannot be substituted for indication-specific trauma treatment.

periop-antifib-rate.question: Tranexamic acid is prepared at 20 mg/mL and administered at the label rate of 2.5 mL/min. What mass rate is delivered?
choices: 5 mg/min
8 mg/min
100 mg/min
50 mg/min
periop-antifib-rate.rationale: 20 mg/mL times 2.5 mL/min equals 50 mg/min. Concentration must accompany a volumetric rate. Five mg/min and 8 mg/min do not equal the concentration multiplied by the stated rate. One hundred mg/min is twice this rate; it is the undiluted label upper limit, not the mass rate in this diluted preparation.

periop-antifib-seizure.question: A patient receiving high-dose IV tranexamic acid develops seizure with impaired renal function. Which assumption should be rejected?
choices: Renal function affects exposure
Seizure risk exists only after accidental spinal administration
Dose and indication need reassessment
Neurologic monitoring is relevant
periop-antifib-seizure.rationale: The label also reports seizures with IV surgical use. Neuraxial errors are a severe additional risk, not the only setting. The rejected statement is the claim that seizure risk exists only with spinal administration. Kidney function affects exposure; reassessing dose and indication and monitoring neurologic status remain appropriate with IV treatment.

periop-antifib-urinary.question: Aminocaproic acid is proposed for upper-urinary-tract hematuria. Which concern requires review before treatment?
choices: It always dissolves obstructing clots
Urinary bleeding is unrelated to antifibrinolysis
Stabilized clots can obstruct the renal pelvis or ureters
Renal clearance eliminates every safety concern
periop-antifib-urinary.rationale: The label warns against use in upper-tract hematuria unless benefit outweighs the obstruction risk. Aminocaproic acid inhibits fibrinolysis rather than dissolving a clot. Urinary bleeding can involve fibrinolysis, but that does not remove the upper-tract warning. Renal elimination does not prevent obstruction or guarantee safety.

periop-antifib-dilution.question: A 250 mg/mL aminocaproic-acid vial is supplied for a prescribed 5-g initial dose. Which preparation statement is correct?
choices: Withdraw 20 mL and prepare the prescribed diluted infusion over the first hour
Inject 20 mL undiluted rapidly
Withdraw 2 mL for a 5-g dose
Replace the initial infusion with an intrathecal injection
periop-antifib-dilution.rationale: 5 g is 5000 mg; dividing by 250 mg/mL gives 20 mL of stock. The label requires dilution and discourages rapid undiluted IV injection. Two mL supplies only 500 mg, one tenth of 5 g. Rapid undiluted injection can cause hypotension, bradycardia or arrhythmia. Intrathecal injection is not this product’s labeled IV infusion route.

periop-txa-trauma-timing.question: An adult arrives 90 minutes after injury with major bleeding. Under the 2023 European trauma guideline, should TXA wait for viscoelastic confirmation of hyperfibrinolysis?
choices: Yes, always await the result
No; start the eligible trauma regimen promptly while resuscitation continues
Use the hemophilia dental schedule instead
Wait until 3 hours have elapsed
periop-txa-trauma-timing.rationale: Recommendation 23 supports early TXA within 3 hours of injury and advises against waiting for viscoelastic results. The regimen is 1 g over 10 minutes followed by 1 g over 8 hours. Waiting for the assay or deliberately waiting until three hours delays recommended early treatment. The multiday hemophilia dental regimen is a different indication and is not the trauma schedule.

periop-txa-postpartum-repeat.question: TXA 1 g IV was completed for postpartum hemorrhage within 3 hours of birth. Bleeding is still ongoing 40 minutes later despite concurrent care. Which TXA step matches WHO treatment guidance, assuming no contraindication?
choices: Automatically start the 8-hour trauma infusion
Switch to a multiday dental regimen
A second 1 g IV dose
Wait until the next day
periop-txa-postpartum-repeat.rationale: WHO permits another 1 g when bleeding persists after 30 minutes or returns within 24 hours of the first dose ending. Maintain the rest of the hemorrhage treatment bundle. The repeat dose is administered over 10 minutes. Neither the trauma infusion nor the multiday dental schedule is the WHO postpartum regimen. Ongoing bleeding after the stated interval does not call for waiting until the next day.

periop-pph-early-recognition.question: After vaginal birth, objectively measured blood loss is 350 mL and pulse is 112/min. Which interpretation fits WHO 2025 first-response criteria?
choices: Wait until blood loss reaches 1000 mL
The measured loss plus abnormal pulse supports prompt first-response treatment
The criteria mandate immediate hysterectomy
TXA alone replaces the treatment bundle
periop-pph-early-recognition.rationale: At least 300 mL with an abnormal hemodynamic sign meets the WHO therapeutic threshold. Pulse above 100/min qualifies. Initiate timely care and assess the cause; these criteria do not automatically determine surgery. Waiting for 1000 mL misses this earlier treatment threshold. It does not mandate hysterectomy; escalation depends on the response and cause. TXA is one component of the care bundle, alongside uterotonics, fluids, examination and escalation.

periop-pph-prophylaxis.question: A proposal would add TXA to every uncomplicated vaginal birth to replace prophylactic oxytocin. How does WHO 2025 inform this proposal?
choices: Routine TXA is preferred because it contracts the uterus
TXA should replace all uterotonics
WHO advises against routine TXA prophylaxis; retain appropriate uterotonic prevention
The treatment recommendation proves universal prophylactic benefit
periop-pph-prophylaxis.rationale: TXA inhibits fibrinolysis and is not a uterotonic. WHO recommends it for PPH treatment but advises against routine prevention at vaginal or cesarean birth. TXA does not contract the uterus and cannot replace uterotonic prevention. Evidence supporting treatment of established hemorrhage does not establish benefit from giving it routinely at every uncomplicated birth.

periop-topical-thrombin-route.question: A RECOTHROM transfer syringe is placed among IV medicines. What action addresses the error?
choices: Inject it through a filter
Stop and restore topical-only identification and handling
Use a lower IV dose
Wait for the INR before injecting
periop-topical-thrombin-route.rationale: RECOTHROM must not enter the circulation; the syringe transfers product for surface application. A filter or a lower dose cannot convert topical thrombin into an IV medicine. Waiting for INR does not establish a safe IV route. Its entry into the circulation can cause thrombosis.

periop-bovine-thrombin-antibodies.question: A patient has suspected antibodies to bovine thrombin after prior exposure. Which product requires avoidance of re-exposure?
choices: Every crystalloid solution
All local anesthetics
THROMBIN-JMI
All red-cell products
periop-bovine-thrombin-antibodies.rationale: THROMBIN-JMI labeling prohibits re-exposure with known or suspected antibodies to bovine thrombin or factor V. This restriction belongs to the bovine thrombin product; it is not a blanket prohibition on crystalloids, local anesthetics or red-cell products. Factor V antibodies may cross-react with human factor V and cause bleeding.

periop-factor-vii-inr.question: After NOVOSEVEN RT, INR normalizes but visible bleeding continues. What should guide assessment?
choices: INR proves treatment success
Ignore observed blood loss
Stop monitoring after laboratory correction
Assess continuing clinical bleeding and the underlying cause
periop-factor-vii-inr.rationale: INR correction does not directly predict hemostatic success. Visible bleeding requires continuing assessment despite laboratory correction. Neither ignoring blood loss nor stopping monitoring is appropriate. The label states that these coagulation parameters do not directly predict hemostasis.

periop-fibrin-spray-distance.question: During TISSEEL application, the team cannot assure the device-specific minimum spray distance. What is appropriate?
choices: Increase gas pressure
Spray closer for stronger adhesion
Do not spray under these conditions; select a suitable labeled application approach
Substitute intravascular injection
periop-fibrin-spray-distance.rationale: Unsafe spray conditions can cause gas embolism. Device, gas, pressure and distance requirements are part of administration safety. Raising gas pressure or moving closer can increase rather than solve the hazard. Intravascular injection is contraindicated. Use a suitable approved delivery method rather than spraying without an assured minimum distance.

periop-factor-product-match.question: Which product-to-disorder pairing is correct?
choices: ADYNOVATE for hereditary factor X deficiency
COAGADEX for hereditary factor X deficiency
FEIBA as routine replacement without inhibitors
Topical thrombin as IV factor VIII replacement
periop-factor-product-match.rationale: COAGADEX is factor X replacement. ADYNOVATE is factor VIII replacement; FEIBA addresses inhibitor-associated hemophilia. ADYNOVATE supplies factor VIII for hemophilia A, not factor X. FEIBA is not labeled for factor-deficiency bleeding without factor VIII or IX inhibitors. Topical thrombin must not be injected and is not factor VIII replacement.

periop-feiba-antifibrinolytic.question: A patient received FEIBA two hours ago. A new order calls for systemic tranexamic acid. Which response best addresses the interaction?
choices: Administer because both agents reduce bleeding
Clarify with hematology before administration because this interval falls within the label warning
Use the INR alone to approve the combination
Switch to aminocaproic acid to eliminate the interaction
periop-feiba-antifibrinolytic.rationale: The FEIBA label discourages systemic antifibrinolytics within approximately 6 to 12 hours after administration because of thrombosis risk; aminocaproic acid shares this concern. A shared bleeding indication does not establish a safe combination. INR alone cannot resolve thrombotic interaction risk. Switching to aminocaproic acid retains the systemic antifibrinolytic concern.

periop-factor-inhibitor-response.question: After an appropriate COAGADEX dose, factor X activity remains below the expected level and bleeding persists. Which evaluation belongs in the reassessment?
choices: Assume a normal INR excludes further evaluation
Replace factor X with topical thrombin intravenously
Evaluate factor X inhibitors along with administration and the bleeding source
Treat all factor products as interchangeable
periop-factor-inhibitor-response.rationale: Failure to achieve expected factor X activity or control bleeding warrants factor X inhibitor testing. This supplements assessment of delivery and the clinical cause. A normal INR cannot exclude an inhibitor or replace factor X activity assessment. Topical thrombin is not an IV replacement option. Products addressing different factors or inhibitor states are not interchangeable.

periop-famotidine-renal-delirium.question: An older ICU patient on famotidine develops delirium as creatinine clearance falls to 25 mL/min. What belongs in the immediate medication assessment?
choices: Continue the original dose because H2 blockers have no CNS effects
Diagnose drug-induced delirium without considering other causes
Review renal dosing and ongoing indication while evaluating other delirium causes
Increase famotidine to compensate for reduced clearance
periop-famotidine-renal-delirium.rationale: Reduced renal clearance increases famotidine exposure; CNS reactions have been reported in older adults and renal impairment. The medication review complements a broader delirium assessment. Continuing without review ignores reduced clearance and the labeled CNS warning. A medication association alone does not establish the cause of delirium. Increasing the dose when clearance falls can increase exposure rather than compensate for it.

newQuestions.question: A RECOTHROM transfer syringe is placed among IV medicines. What action addresses the error?
choices: Inject it through a filter
Stop and restore topical-only identification and handling
Use a lower IV dose
Wait for the INR before injecting
newQuestions.rationale: RECOTHROM must not enter the circulation; the syringe transfers product for surface application. A filter or a lower dose cannot convert topical thrombin into an IV medicine. Waiting for INR does not establish a safe IV route. Its entry into the circulation can cause thrombosis.

newQuestions.question: A patient has suspected antibodies to bovine thrombin after prior exposure. Which product requires avoidance of re-exposure?
choices: Every crystalloid solution
All local anesthetics
THROMBIN-JMI
All red-cell products
newQuestions.rationale: THROMBIN-JMI labeling prohibits re-exposure with known or suspected antibodies to bovine thrombin or factor V. This restriction belongs to the bovine thrombin product; it is not a blanket prohibition on crystalloids, local anesthetics or red-cell products. Factor V antibodies may cross-react with human factor V and cause bleeding.

newQuestions.question: After NOVOSEVEN RT, INR normalizes but visible bleeding continues. What should guide assessment?
choices: INR proves treatment success
Ignore observed blood loss
Stop monitoring after laboratory correction
Assess continuing clinical bleeding and the underlying cause
newQuestions.rationale: INR correction does not directly predict hemostatic success. Visible bleeding requires continuing assessment despite laboratory correction. Neither ignoring blood loss nor stopping monitoring is appropriate. The label states that these coagulation parameters do not directly predict hemostasis.

newQuestions.question: During TISSEEL application, the team cannot assure the device-specific minimum spray distance. What is appropriate?
choices: Increase gas pressure
Spray closer for stronger adhesion
Do not spray under these conditions; select a suitable labeled application approach
Substitute intravascular injection
newQuestions.rationale: Unsafe spray conditions can cause gas embolism. Device, gas, pressure and distance requirements are part of administration safety. Raising gas pressure or moving closer can increase rather than solve the hazard. Intravascular injection is contraindicated. Use a suitable approved delivery method rather than spraying without an assured minimum distance.

choices: ADYNOVATE for hereditary factor X deficiency

FEIBA as routine replacement without inhibitors
